related_questions.question: What is considered chronic diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: Chronic diabetes conditions include type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. Potentially reversible diabetes conditions include prediabetes and gestational diabetes. Prediabetes happens when blood sugar levels are higher than normal. But the blood sugar levels aren't high enough to be called diabetes.

related_questions.question: How to get diabetes medicine for free?

text_blocks.snippet: To obtain free diabetes medication, explore patient assistance programs offered by pharmaceutical companies, state programs, or non-profits. These programs have specific eligibility requirements, often based on income and insurance status. Additionally, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) provides resources for finding help with medication costs, including connecting you with manufacturers' programs and local resources.
snippet_highlighted_words: explore patient assistance programs offered by pharmaceutical companies, state programs, or non-profits

list.title: Major Insulin Manufacturers:
list.snippet: Many companies like Lilly, Sanofi, and Novo Nordisk offer patient assistance programs (PAPs) providing free or low-cost insulin for those who qualify.

list.title: Eligibility:
list.snippet: These programs typically require proof of income, lack of insurance, or underinsurance, and may have income limits related to the federal poverty level.

list.title: Application Process:
list.snippet: Each program has its own application process, often involving financial documentation and proof of residency.

list.title: Resources:
list.snippet: The ADA provides resources to find programs from specific insulin manufacturers.

list.title: State Programs:
list.snippet: Explore your state's Medicaid or other programs designed to help with medication costs.

list.title: Non-Profit Organizations:
list.snippet: Organizations like the National Association of Free & Charitable Clinics offer access to free or low-cost clinics that can provide diabetes medications.

list.title: Resources:
list.snippet: The ADA provides access to local resources for medical care, advocacy, and more.

list.title: Generic Alternatives:
list.snippet: Consider generic alternatives to your prescribed medication, which can be significantly cheaper.

list.title: Savings Programs:
list.snippet: Check for savings programs or coupons offered by pharmacies or drug manufacturers.

list.title: Community Health Centers:
list.snippet: Many community health centers offer discounted medications and services.

list.title: NeedyMeds:
list.snippet: This website provides information on patient assistance programs and other resources for managing medication costs.

list.title: GoFundMe:
list.snippet: If you are struggling to afford your medications, consider setting up a GoFundMe campaign to help offset costs.

list.title: Talk to Your Doctor:
list.snippet: Discuss your financial concerns with your doctor or healthcare team. They can help you find resources and explore options.

list.title: Contact the Manufacturer Directly:
list.snippet: Reach out to the manufacturer of your specific medication to inquire about their patient assistance programs.

list.title: Gather Necessary Documents:
list.snippet: Prepare financial documents like tax returns, pay stubs, and insurance information for the application process.

list.title: Be Patient:
list.snippet: Applying for patient assistance programs can take time. Be patient and persistent throughout the process.

related_questions.question: What are the complications of chronic diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: Complications of diabetes include eye problems, foot problems, heart attacks, nerve damage, and other chronic (long-term) issues. There are also acute complications (short-term) including hypos and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). But there are things you can do to prevent complications.
related_questions.title: Complications of diabetes | Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes

related_questions.question: Is chronic diabetes curable?
related_questions.snippet: There's no cure for type 2 diabetes. Losing weight, eating well and exercising can help manage the condition. If diet and exercise aren't enough to manage blood sugar, diabetes medicines or insulin therapy may help.
